extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and critics of poetry (particularly Milton's Paradise Lost)
extracted.subtask_description: Literary-critical guidance and evaluative principles for judging/understanding epic poetry, illustrated by commentary on Milton's Paradise Lost. Emphasizes diction, description, character-speech, use of classical models, and the function of poetical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornamented diction reserved for idle parts (Aristotle's rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted footnote guidance: 'The diction should be most laboured in the idle parts of the poem; those in which neither manners nor sentiments prevail; for the manners and the sentiments are only obscured by too splendid a diction.' Use elaborate, florid expression where manners/sentiments do not dominate; avoid splendid diction where sentiment and character should speak plainly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and scope of descriptive passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions (e.g., of Paradise) must be particular when the scene is the principal action and when they are needed to give an idea of the happiness or condition depicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While drawings of gardens, rivers, etc., are 'justly censured' in an heroic poem when they run into unnecessary length, the Description of Paradise is justified because it is the scene of the principal action and requisite to convey the happiness from which the first parents fell. Descriptive excess is fault if gratuitous; it is proper when it serves the fable or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting-consistent thought and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters' sentiments and allusions should reflect their habitation and condition (e.g., Adam and Eve's thoughts are 'always Paradisiacal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain that speakers continually bear the tincture of their environment—just as shepherds' thoughts take a pastoral tinge, the first parents' language and imagination should continually reference Paradise. This coherence strengthens characterization throughout the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artful construction of machines/plot devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Machines (the poetical devices and contrivances of the plot) should be raised with art to connect the series of adventures and to produce agreeable surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Satan's bounding over Paradise walls, his transformations to overhear conversation, and his various disguises are praised as circumstances that give agreeable surprise and are devised with great art to connect adventures. Devices must integrate with the narrative and propel the fable, not feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speeches must reflect changing passions and character
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker's language should mirror his or her immediate perceptions and moral condition (e.g., Satan's speech to the Sun shows transient remorse then confirmed impenitence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good speeches show progression of feeling (remorse → self-accusation → impenitence) and are 'raised with a great deal of Art.' Opening lines may be bold and noble; conferences should contain sentiments proper to each speaker and occasion, demonstrating psychological truth and rhetorical fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical borrowings should serve the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's use of hints and literal translations from Greek and Latin poets is acceptable when it aids the fable; imitation should not be mere ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: weighing events in scales (from Homer/Virgil) is used not only as embellishment but to break off a combat and carry on the fable. Reserve learned borrowing for moments where it furthers plot or moral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trivial prettiness beneath the poet's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Fanciful or pretty devices (e.g., Uriel gliding on a sunbeam) may be admired in a little fanciful poet but are beneath the genius of a great poet like Milton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between sublime inventions and merely 'pretty' conceits; the latter can diminish the authority of a great poet if used inappropriately. Evaluate whether a device is dignified enough for the poet's stature and the work's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity and liveliness in celestial/angelic depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of angelic hosts, their nightly rounds, and hymns should be drawn with strength, liveliness, and the divine—'inexpressibly amusing to the Imagination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such passages require a different spirit from smaller fanciful conceits: aim for grandeur, vivid motion ('dazling the Moon'), and language that evokes awe rather than trifle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of passion and dignity in love-speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Professions of love should be full of warmth yet founded on truth; the man may speak endearing things without descending from natural dignity, the woman receive them without departing from modesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose romantic dialogue so both speakers preserve their character: Adam retains elevated dignity while expressing tenderness; Eve shows modesty and sincerity. Avoid hyperbole or artifice that would undermine character or seem improper for a state of innocence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual subordination must be maintained in characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The mutual subordination of the sexes is 'wonderfully kept up' in the poem; each partner appears in its proper force and loveliness without violating their roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting relationships, keep consistent social/character hierarchies that the poem's moral or aesthetic order requires; this balance is part of the poem's artistry in representing innocence and harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of surprise with moral significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations and sudden revelations (e.g., Satan's starting up in his own form) should combine literal description with a concealed moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devices ought to yield both sensory surprise and moral insight; an episode's literal vividness should also carry ethical or allegorical weight so the description contributes to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural beginning of speeches without awkward omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating the Ancients by beginning a speech without 'he said' requires judgment so the omission is not missed and the speech begins naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slavish imitation of classical habits unless the omission flows naturally; a successful classical-style opening feels unforced and preserves clarity of speech attribution.
